newsitem.title: BARBADOS: Clinton says House crime bill ignores his plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says House crime bill ignores his plan.

text.p: President Clinton Saturday attacked juvenile crime legislation passed by the Republican-controlled House of Representatives, saying it ignores his own prescription for stopping youth violence.

"I challenge Congress to pass a real juvenile justice bill, one that's tough on gangs and tough on guns and is serious about the kind of prevention efforts we know will work," he said in his weekly radio address.

The House approved juvenile justice legislation Thursday by a vote of 286 to 132 with 77 Democrats joining 209 Republicans. It would allow juveniles as young as 13 to be tried as adults for violent crimes and drug offences.
The bill would only apply to federal crimes, which account for a small percentage of overall offences. But supporters said it was needed to encourage states to also try violent juveniles as adults.

Clinton, on a week-long tour of Mexico, Costa Rica and Barbados, complained the House bill ignored the anti-crime measures he proposed in legislation sent to Congress in February to crack down on youth gangs.

Clinton, who made fighting juvenile crime and gangs a top priority of his second term, did not specifically threaten a veto of the House bill. A similar bill is pending in the Republican-led Senate. Clinton and the Republicans have fought frequently over the direction of crime-fighting measures.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton would "fight hard for our strategy. We think over time we'll be able to win the case on the merits of our argument."

The president's legislation would "declare war" on gangs with new prosecutors and tougher penalties. It would extend the Brady Bill handgun control law to bar someone who commits a crime as a juvenile from buying a gun as an adult.

It would also require that child-safety locks be sold with guns to try to prevent accidental shootings and it would help keep schools open after hours, on weekends and in the summer to give children a place to go to instead of hitting the streets.
Clinton said the House bill does not ensure the anti-gang prosecutors, is weak on guns, and does not fund his initiatives to keep schools open.

Perhaps most troubling, he said, the House bill rejects his call to cut off young people's access to guns, which he said was now the third leading cause of death for young people between the ages of 13 and 24.
As for the child-safety locks, Clinton cited a National Institute of Justice survey that said 185 children died in 194 because of accidental shootings.
"Now, if we can have safety precautions to prevent children from opening bottles of aspirin, surely we can have the same safety precautions to prevent children from using guns," Clinton said.
Clinton taped his radio address Friday aboard Air Force One while sitting on the tarmac at the airport in San Jose, Costa Rica.
The White House and the Republicans also clashed Saturday on their different versions of legislation to give working parents more time off from work to be with their children.

"The Republican Congress will help hard-pressed families in a very simple way -- we can give them more time together as a family," said Sen. Bill Frist of Tennessee in the weekly Republican radio address.
The Republican bill would allow workers and employers to agree on flexible work schedules and let employees take compensatory time off in place of extra pay for overtime.
The bill, called the Family-Friendly Workplace Act, or the flex-time bill, has passed the House and is being considered by the Senate.
But labour unions oppose the measure, saying it would be used to pressure workers to take compensatory time off rather than overtime pay and weaken the standard 40-hour work week.
Clinton has vowed to veto the legislation. He has his own legislative proposal to give workers two days off a year to attend parent-teacher conferences or take children to the doctor.

"Theirs is a comp time bill," said White House spokeswoman Mary Ellen Glynn. "Basically what we want to make certain is that employers can't force employees to take comp time when they want to take overtime.
"In our bill, if an employee wants to take comp time they can take comp time, and if they want to take overtime they can take overtime. We want to preserve worker choice," she said.
